Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Sen. Hillary Clinton will stop telling an emotional story about a uninsured pregnant woman who died after being denied medical care, Clinton's campaign said. Sen. Hillary Clinton was repeating a story she heard from someone on the campaign trail. A hospital has raised questions over the accuracy of the story, and Clinton's campaign has said although they had no reason to doubt the story, they were unable to confirm the details. In the story, Clinton describes a woman from rural Ohio who was making minimum wage at a local pizza shop. The woman, who was uninsured, became pregnant. Clinton said the woman ran into trouble and went to a hospital in a nearby county but was denied treatment because she couldn't afford a $100 payment. In her speeches, Clinton said the woman later was taken to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The young woman was then taken by helicopter to a Columbus hospital where she died of complications.  Watch why the story is raising questions » . The New York senator heard the story during a campaign visit to a family's living room in Pomeroy, Ohio, in late February. Bryan Holman was hosting the candidate and told Clinton the story. She has repeated it frequently since then. As recently as Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said she was "just aching inside" as she was listening to the story. "It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn't have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined," she said. While Clinton never named the hospital in her speech, the woman she was referring to was treated at O'Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman did indeed have insurance, and, at least at their hospital, she was never turned away. Hospital Chief Executive Officer Rick Castrop in a statement said, "we reviewed the medical and patient accounts of the patient" after she was named in a newspaper story about Clinton's stump speech. "There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman." A hospital spokesperson confirmed to CNN the woman had insurance. She said the hospital decided to come forward after people in the community began to question if they had denied her care. Clinton's speech accurately reflects what she was told that day, but the campaign admits they were not able to confirm the account. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said, "She had no reason to doubt his word." "Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it's common for candidates to retell those stories. It's not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren't able to fully vet the story," he said. Elleithee added, "If the hospital claims it didn't happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won't repeat the story." "She never mentions the hospital by name and isn't trying to cast blame. She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That's a point very few people will dispute." E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** Sen. Hillary Clinton will stop recounting an emotional story about an uninsured pregnant woman who died after allegedly being denied medical care, her campaign said.

Clinton had been repeating a story she heard from someone on the campaign trail. A hospital has since raised questions about the account’s accuracy, and Clinton’s campaign said that, although it had no reason to doubt the story, it was unable to confirm the details.

In the story, Clinton describes a woman from rural Ohio who earned minimum wage at a local pizza shop. The uninsured woman became pregnant and later experienced complications. According to Clinton, she went to a hospital in a neighboring county but was denied treatment because she could not afford a $100 payment.

In her speeches, Clinton said the woman was later taken to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The young woman was then transported by helicopter to a hospital in Columbus, where she died from complications.

**Watch why the story is raising questions »**

The New York senator first heard the story in late February during a campaign visit to a family’s living room in Pomeroy, Ohio. Bryan Holman, who was hosting the candidate, told Clinton the story, which she has frequently repeated since then.

As recently as Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said she was “just aching inside” as she listened to the account.

“It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn’t have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined,” she said.

Although Clinton never identified the hospital in her speech, the woman to whom she was referring was treated at O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman did, in fact, have insurance and that, at least at its facility, she was never turned away.

Hospital Chief Executive Officer Rick Castrop said in a statement that the hospital had “reviewed the medical and patient accounts of the patient” after she was identified in a newspaper story about Clinton’s stump speech.

“There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman,” Castrop said.

A hospital spokesperson confirmed to CNN that the woman had insurance. She said the hospital decided to speak publicly after members of the community began questioning whether it had denied the woman care.

Clinton’s speech accurately reflected what she had been told that day, but her campaign acknowledged that it had been unable to confirm the account.

“She had no reason to doubt his word,” Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said.

“Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it’s common for candidates to retell those stories. It’s not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren’t able to fully vet the story,” he said.

Elleithee added, “If the hospital claims it didn’t happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won’t repeat the story.”

“She never mentions the hospital by name and isn’t trying to cast blame. She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That’s a point very few people will dispute.”

Clinton learned of the case from a man she met while campaigning. Although her staff said there had been no initial reason to question his account, it acknowledged that it could not verify the details. A hospital connected to the case has since challenged the story’s accuracy.

In Clinton’s version, a pregnant woman in rural Ohio was earning minimum wage at a neighborhood pizza restaurant and had no health insurance. After experiencing medical problems, she went to a hospital in a neighboring county but was allegedly turned away because she could not pay $100. Clinton said the woman was later transported to the hospital by ambulance and lost her baby. She was then flown by helicopter to a hospital in Columbus, where she died from complications. Watch why the account is being questioned »

Clinton first heard the story in late February while visiting a family’s home in Pomeroy, Ohio, during a campaign stop. Her host, Bryan Holman, related the account to her, and she repeated it often afterward.

As recently as Friday evening in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said hearing the story left her “just aching inside.”

“It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn't have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined,” she said.

Although Clinton did not identify the facility in her speeches, the woman she was discussing received treatment at O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. Hospital officials said she did have insurance and was never refused care there.

In a statement, hospital CEO Rick Castrop said the facility examined the woman’s medical and billing records after a newspaper article about Clinton’s campaign speech identified her.

“There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman,” Castrop said.

A hospital representative also confirmed to CNN that the woman was insured. According to the spokesperson, the hospital chose to respond publicly after community members began asking whether it had refused to treat her.

Clinton accurately repeated what she had been told during the Ohio visit, but her campaign conceded that it had been unable to substantiate the account.

Her spokesman, Mo Elleithee, said, “She had no reason to doubt his word.”

“Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it's common for candidates to retell those stories. It's not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren't able to fully vet the story,” he said.

Elleithee added, “If the hospital claims it didn't happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won't repeat the story.”

He also emphasized that Clinton never identified the hospital and was not seeking to assign blame.

“She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That's a point very few people will dispute,” he said.

## Clinton drops health care anecdote after hospital disputes account

**(CNN) —** Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign said the New York senator would stop repeating a stump-speech story about an uninsured pregnant woman who allegedly died after an Ohio hospital refused to treat her because she could not pay a $100 fee.

Clinton had used the anecdote to illustrate problems with the nation’s health care system, telling audiences that the woman was denied care, later lost her baby and then died herself.

But O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio, disputed that account. Hospital officials said the woman had not been refused treatment and had insurance coverage. They also said the facility does not deny emergency care based on a patient’s ability to pay.

The woman was identified in news reports as Trina Bachtel, who died in 2007 after complications related to pregnancy.

Clinton’s campaign said the story had been relayed to her by a local official and acknowledged that it had not independently verified the details before she used it publicly. After the hospital challenged the account, the campaign said Clinton would no longer tell the story.

The episode came as Clinton made expanding health insurance coverage a central issue in her campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination.
